passage: Mohit, you're sixteen and your friends are full of rumours, I can see it. Let me tell you one small thing from when I was seventeen, before nursing college. There was a boy in my tuition, Anil. We liked each other. One evening, on the way home, he stopped and asked, 'Can I hold your hand?' Just like that, asked. I hesitated, and he said, 'Okay, not today then,' and walked on talking about cricket. I admired him so much for that. Asking, and meaning it when the answer isn't yes. Now I work in a clinic, and I see young people hurt by myths about protection and infections that they picked up from friends. So, respect a no, and bring your questions to me or a doctor, not to rumours.

qa.q: What did Anil say when the narrator hesitated?
qa.a: 'Okay, not today then,' and he walked on talking about cricket.

qa.q: Why did the narrator admire Anil so much?
qa.a: He asked before touching them and accepted their hesitation without sulking or pushing.

qa.q: What does the narrator want Mohit to do with questions about sexual health?
qa.a: Bring them to the narrator or a doctor, rather than trusting rumours from friends.

qa.q: How might Anil's response have felt different if he had just grabbed the narrator's hand?
qa.a: The narrator would likely have felt uncomfortable and disrespected instead of safe and admiring.

grounding: An elder recalls a boy asking and respecting a hesitant answer, and urges reliable sexual health information.

passage: The health workshop got cut short when the fire drill rang, so Nurse Farida only had twenty minutes left. She quickly opened the anonymous question box instead. Gautam, seventeen, had written one: 'If someone says no but is smiling, does it still mean no?' His hand was sweaty folding it. She read it out. A few boys sniggered. 'Yes. No means no. Smiling can mean nervous or polite. If you're unsure, ask, and if it's not a clear yes, stop.' She covered facts about protection and infections quickly, pointing students to the school doctor for private questions. At lunch, Bunty joked, 'Girls say no to play hard to get.' Jaya rolled her eyes. Before she could speak, Gautam said, 'Nurse said no means no. Doesn't matter if she's smiling.' Jaya nodded at him.

qa.q: Why did Nurse Farida only have twenty minutes left?
qa.a: The workshop got cut short when the fire drill rang.

qa.q: Why do you think Gautam's hand was sweaty when he folded his question?
qa.a: He was nervous and maybe embarrassed to ask, but he genuinely wanted to understand consent.

qa.q: Which part of the nurse's answer is most useful for teens?
qa.a: That a smile doesn't mean yes, and if it isn't a clear yes, you ask or stop.

qa.q: How might Jaya see Gautam after he answered Bunty's joke?
qa.a: She would likely respect him for repeating what he learned and standing up for girls' no.

grounding: Shows teens learning that no means no and getting basic sexual health facts from a trusted source despite time pressure.

passage:
Vikas,
I'm writing this because every time I try to say it, you talk over me.
When we started going around, you were funny and kind. But these past months, you've asked for my phone password, you get angry when I go to Ishita's house, and you text 'where are you' twenty times if I don't reply. You call it caring. It doesn't feel like caring. It feels like I'm being watched.
I talked to my masi about it, and she asked me one question: 'Do you feel freer or smaller with him?' Smaller. That's my answer.
I want someone who trusts me without checking. I hope you learn that too, for whoever comes next.
I'm ending this. Please don't come to my house.
Sunaina

qa.q: What did Vikas ask Sunaina for that she mentions first?
qa.a: He asked for her phone password.

qa.q: What does Sunaina's answer 'Smaller' reveal about how she felt in the relationship?
qa.a: She felt controlled and diminished, not loved, because of his checking and anger.

qa.q: What was wise about Sunaina talking to her masi?
qa.a: A trusted adult helped her see the pattern clearly with one simple question, so she could decide for herself.

qa.q: How might Vikas see his own behaviour if he truly reads the letter?
qa.a: He might realise that what he called caring felt like surveillance and control to her.

grounding: A teen writes a letter recognising possessive, controlling behaviour and choosing freedom and respect.

passage: This is kind of embarrassing, but here goes, since you asked on the podcast. I'm Santosh, seventeen. Last year I was going out with Hansa, and I thought I was a great boyfriend. I texted her all day. If she didn't reply in ten minutes, I'd get this burning feeling and send more. I got annoyed when she hung out with her cousin's friends. Then one day she said, 'It feels like a leash, Santosh.' I was so offended. I sulked for two days. Then I read our chats from start to finish. I sounded like a guard, not a friend. I apologised. We're not together now, but we're good friends. I learned trust means not checking.

qa.q: What did Hansa say the relationship felt like?
qa.a: She said it felt like a leash.

qa.q: Why did Santosh feel a 'burning feeling' when Hansa didn't reply quickly?
qa.a: He felt anxious and jealous, and he treated her silence as something to control.

qa.q: What helped Santosh see the problem in his behaviour?
qa.a: Reading their chats from start to finish let him see that he sounded like a guard, not a caring friend.

qa.q: How might Hansa have felt during the months of constant texts?
qa.a: She probably felt watched and pressured, less free to see friends without explaining herself.

grounding: A teen recounts recognising his own possessive behaviour as control and changing it.

passage:
Dear Yusuf,
You asked how I'm doing since Ammamma died. Honestly, I don't know. It's been three weeks. Some days I'm fine and then I hear a pressure cooker whistle and I cry because she always shouted 'Reena, turn it off!' Isn't that silly?
Amma gave me her green shawl. I sleep with it. It still smells of her coconut oil.
On Sunday, I tried making her tomato rasam from memory. It was too sour, and Appa laughed, and then he cried too. We sat in the kitchen together for a long time. That helped more than anything.
I've started writing down her sayings in a notebook so I don't forget.
Write back soon. Tell me about your new school.
Reena

qa.q: What did Amma give Reena that belonged to Ammamma?
qa.a: Her green shawl, which still smells of her coconut oil.

qa.q: Why did Reena cry when she heard a pressure cooker whistle?
qa.a: It reminded Reena of Ammamma shouting 'Reena, turn it off!', bringing the loss back suddenly.

qa.q: Which of Reena's ways of mourning could help other grieving teens?
qa.a: Keeping a meaningful object, cooking a family recipe and writing down the person's sayings.

qa.q: How might Appa have felt in the kitchen after laughing at the rasam?
qa.a: He was grieving Ammamma too, and sharing the moment with Reena let his own tears come.

grounding: A teen writes about grieving a grandmother and the ways the family mourns.

passage: You know how everyone says 'it was just a cat'? Mitthu wasn't just a cat to me. I'm Preeti, I'm sixteen, and I had him since I was seven. Last month he got sick and the vet said he was very old. My brother Vijay and I sat with him on the balcony till the end. After that, I didn't want to talk to anyone. At school a girl said, 'Get a new one,' and I wanted to scream. What helped? Vijay and I buried him under the neem tree and planted marigolds. I made a small photo album. And I let myself cry in the shower without feeling stupid. It's still sore, but lighter. I talk to him sometimes. Is that weird?

qa.q: Where did Preeti and Vijay bury Mitthu?
qa.a: Under the neem tree, where they planted marigolds.

qa.q: How did Preeti feel when a girl told her to 'get a new one'?
qa.a: Preeti was angry and hurt, because the comment dismissed how much Mitthu meant.

qa.q: What helped Preeti mourn in a healthy way?
qa.a: Burying him with a small ritual, making a photo album and allowing tears without shame.

qa.q: If you were the girl who said 'Get a new one', what would a kinder response have been?
qa.a: Saying 'I'm sorry, you had him for so long' would acknowledge that Preeti's grief was real.

grounding: A teen tells how they grieved a pet and found ways to mourn.

passage: Devika, you ask why I'm happy walking alone every morning? Let me explain the difference, because I learned it the hard way. At fifteen I loved going alone to the lake with my sketchbook to draw herons. Hours alone, and I came home full, like after a good meal. Then my father got transferred to a new city. I stopped talking at school. I ate lunch in the library, not because I wanted to, but because I was afraid of the other boys. At home I shut my door. That aloneness felt hollow, like hunger. My mother noticed and found a birdwatching club at the park. I went, sulking. By the third Sunday I had a friend. So ask yourself, beta: does your alone time feed you, or empty you?

qa.q: What did the narrator draw at the lake as a teen?
qa.a: Herons, in a sketchbook.

qa.q: How did the narrator's aloneness feel different after the move?
qa.a: It felt hollow and empty because he was hiding out of fear, not choosing to be alone.

qa.q: What question does the narrator give Devika about time spent alone?
qa.a: Whether that alone time feeds Devika or empties Devika.

qa.q: How might the narrator's mother have felt noticing her son shut in his room?
qa.a: She was likely worried about him and wanted to find a gentle way to help him connect.

grounding: An elder contrasts healthy solitude with painful isolation and how he acted on it.

passage: The Diwali bus tickets home had doubled in price, so Hemant, sixteen, stayed back in the Kota hostel while everyone else left. The first evening felt like a treat. No noise, no one knocking. He read a whole novel on his bed and ate instant noodles from the canteen. The second day, the corridor echoed. He scrolled through photos of friends lighting diyas with their families, and something in his chest went tight. By the third evening he hadn't spoken to a single person in two days. He realised the quiet had turned from peaceful to heavy. So he called Omkar, who laughed and put him on video with his whole family. Then Hemant went downstairs and asked the guard if he'd like to share some sweets.

qa.q: Why did Hemant stay back in the hostel?
qa.a: The Diwali bus tickets home had doubled in price.

qa.q: What does the tight feeling in Hemant's chest suggest?
qa.a: Seeing friends with their families made him feel lonely and left out.

qa.q: How did Hemant act once he noticed the quiet had become heavy?
qa.a: He reached out by calling Omkar and then went to share sweets with the guard.

qa.q: How might the guard have felt when Hemant came down with sweets?
qa.a: He might have been touched to have company on Diwali, possibly away from his own family too. 🙂

grounding: Shows a teen noticing when chosen solitude turns into loneliness and acting on it.

passage: Since the results in April, Kiran, fifteen, had stopped going to the fields in the evenings with the other girls. She sat on the charpai and stared at the tamarind tree. Her mother said she was lazy. Weeks passed like that. One afternoon at the handpump, her friend Salma said, 'You don't even laugh at my jokes. Are you okay?' Kiran felt her eyes fill. 'I feel heavy all the time. Even when nothing is wrong.' Salma held her hand. 'This has been going on too long, Kiran. Let's tell Sister Mercy at school. She knows about these things.' The next day, Sister Mercy listened and said, 'Thank you for telling me. There's a counsellor at the district hospital. We'll talk to your mother together.'

qa.q: Where did Salma talk to Kiran?
qa.a: At the handpump.

qa.q: How did Kiran describe what she was feeling?
qa.a: She said she felt heavy all the time, even when nothing was wrong.

qa.q: Why was Salma's suggestion a good one?
qa.a: She noticed it had lasted a long time and linked Kiran to a trusted adult who could get proper help.

qa.q: How might Kiran's mother see the situation after the meeting?
qa.a: She might realise that what she called laziness was real distress that needed care, not scolding.

grounding: Shows a rural teen recognising persistent sadness and withdrawal and reaching out to trusted adults and a counsellor.

passage: At the girls' hostel in Pune, lights went off at ten-thirty, but Kalyani, sixteen, kept studying with her phone torch under the blanket. Then scrolling. She couldn't fall asleep before one anyway, her body just wasn't tired. In the morning she dragged herself to the six-thirty prayer assembly and dozed off in chemistry twice. Ritu, her roommate, watched this for a week. 'Your body clock's shifted, not broken,' she said. 'Mine too. But the phone makes it worse.' They made a deal: phones in the locker at eleven, heavy chapters before dinner, easy reading after. Kalyani also started walking in the courtyard in the morning sun. It took two weeks, but she stopped nodding off in chemistry.

qa.q: When did lights go off in the hostel?
qa.a: At ten-thirty.

qa.q: How did Kalyani seem to feel about her late nights at first?
qa.a: She felt stuck, since her body wasn't tired before one even though she was exhausted in the mornings.

qa.q: Which parts of Kalyani and Ritu's plan could other teens borrow?
qa.a: Putting phones away at night, moving heavy study earlier and getting morning sunlight.

qa.q: How might the chemistry teacher notice the change in Kalyani?
qa.a: The teacher would see her more alert and awake instead of dozing off in class.

grounding: Shows a teen in a hostel managing a shifted body clock, late-night phone use and study load.

passage:
Dear Bidisha di,
How's college? I have a sleep problem and you're the only one who won't lecture me.
This year my body just won't sleep before one at night. I lie there wide awake while Maa thinks I'm on my phone. Sometimes I am, okay. Then the alarm at six feels like a punch. I read that teen body clocks actually shift later, so it's not only laziness.
Here's what I'm trying: no phone in bed, it charges on the dressing table. Maths early in the evening, when my brain works. Opening the curtains the moment I wake up. On weekends I'm trying not to sleep till noon, which is TORTURE.
It's slightly better. Any tips from hostel life?
Nazia

qa.q: Where does Nazia's phone charge now?
qa.a: On the dressing table, not in bed.

qa.q: Why does Nazia call Bidisha di the only one who won't lecture?
qa.a: Nazia feels misunderstood at home, since Maa assumes it's only the phone, and trusts Bidisha di to listen.

qa.q: What is sensible about Nazia's plan?
qa.a: It works with a shifted body clock by moving hard study earlier, cutting phone use in bed and using morning light.

qa.q: How might Maa's view change if Maa read this letter?
qa.a: Maa might understand Nazia's late nights aren't only laziness and support Nazia's plan instead of blaming.

grounding: A teen writes about a shifted sleep clock, late-night use and study load, and a plan to manage them.

passage: I'm Lakshmi, Sangeeta's cousin. At my sister's wedding in Coimbatore, the older boys had a table behind the tent with bottles hidden under a tablecloth. I saw one of them wave Sangeeta over. She's sixteen. He poured something into a paper cup and held it out, laughing. She shook her head and held up the lime soda already in her hand. I couldn't hear everything, but I caught, 'No thanks, I'm on dance duty, need my feet.' He pushed the cup closer. She laughed, said it again, and walked off to the dance floor without looking back. Later I asked if she was okay. She shrugged and said, 'I practised saying that in the mirror.' I don't know if she was nervous. She didn't look it.

qa.q: What was Sangeeta holding when the cup was offered?
qa.a: A lime soda.

qa.q: How can you tell Sangeeta felt ready for such a moment?
qa.a: She seemed confident and prepared: she had practised her refusal line in the mirror, then laughed and walked off without looking back.

qa.q: What made Sangeeta's refusal effective?
qa.a: She had a ready, light reason, repeated it calmly when pushed and then walked away.

qa.q: What might the boy with the cup have thought when she walked off?
qa.a: He may have been surprised she didn't give in and realised pushing wasn't going to work.

grounding: An observer sees a teen refuse alcohol at a wedding using a rehearsed line.

passage: Monday: Behind the school canteen, two seniors were passing around a vape. One held it out to Jomon, fifteen. 'Try it, it's just flavour, mango.' Jomon's face went hot. 'Maybe later,' he mumbled and left, feeling like a coward. Wednesday: At the bus stop he told Avni. She didn't laugh. 'Those things still mess with your lungs, flavour or not. And later means they'll ask again.' They made up lines. 'Nah, I've got football.' 'Not my thing.' Jomon repeated them, feeling silly, then less silly. Friday: The senior held it out again. 'Mango, bro.' 'Nah, not my thing. Football.' Jomon kept walking. Behind him, he heard, 'Whatever.' That was it. His heart was pounding, but he grinned all the way to the field.

qa.q: What flavour did the senior say the vape was?
qa.a: Mango.

qa.q: Why did Jomon feel like a coward on Monday?
qa.a: He felt ashamed because he hadn't said a clear no, only mumbled 'maybe later' and left.

qa.q: What helped Jomon refuse more easily on Friday?
qa.a: Rehearsing short, ready lines with Avni so he didn't have to think on the spot.

qa.q: How might Avni feel when Jomon tells her about Friday?
qa.a: She would likely be happy and proud that the lines they practised worked. 😊

grounding: Over several days a teen learns the risk of vaping and rehearses refusing a peer's offer.

passage: In Berlin, the course choices for the upper school were due Friday. Elif, sixteen, sat at the kitchen table with the form while her father cut apples. 'Biology and chemistry, of course,' he said. 'Doctor. Stable life.' Elif's pen hovered. Her sketchbooks, full of redesigned bus stops and chairs, lay on the windowsill. The aptitude test at school had said she was strong in spatial thinking. Ms Vera, the careers advisor, had said, 'Talk to him with your evidence, not just your feelings.' So Elif opened her sketchbook. 'Baba, I'm good at science, but I lose track of time when I design. Architecture needs both maths and art.' He looked at the bus stops for a long while. 'Show me the test results too.'

qa.q: What did Elif's sketchbooks contain?
qa.a: Redesigned bus stops and chairs.

qa.q: What might Elif have been feeling as her pen hovered over the form?
qa.a: She felt torn between her father's hopes for medicine and her own interest in design.

qa.q: Why was Ms Vera's advice useful for Elif?
qa.a: Bringing her sketchbooks and test results gave her father concrete evidence of her strengths, not just a wish.

qa.q: How might Elif's father see the choice after looking at the sketchbooks?
qa.a: He might begin to see architecture as a serious path that uses her abilities, while still wanting stability for her.

grounding: Shows a teen outside India matching strengths to a stream while weighing a parent's expectations.

passage: The career counselling room at the Jaipur school had a poster of a tree with branches labelled with jobs. Yash, fifteen, sat opposite Aadhya Ma'am with his aptitude report. 'Language and social reasoning, very high,' she said. 'Numerical, average.' Yash looked at his shoes. 'Papa wants me to take science. Everyone in the family did.' 'And you?' 'I like history. And I write for the school paper.' 'Hmm. What do you imagine doing at twenty-five?' He hesitated. 'Maybe journalism. Or law?' 'Both fit your strengths. Shall we invite your father for a meeting? You can show him this report, and I'll explain the options in humanities.' Yash let out a breath. 'Will you be there?' 'Of course.'

qa.q: What were Yash's strongest areas in the aptitude report?
qa.a: Language and social reasoning.

qa.q: Why did Yash look at his shoes when talking about his father?
qa.a: He was worried about disappointing his father and the family tradition of science.

qa.q: What step did Aadhya Ma'am suggest to handle the family expectation?
qa.a: A meeting with his father where Yash could share his report and she could explain humanities options.

qa.q: How might Yash's father feel at the meeting?
qa.a: He might be surprised or anxious at first, but seeing the evidence could help him support Yash's choice.

grounding: Shows a teen matching his aptitude and interests to a stream while weighing family input with a counsellor.

passage:

Since you just got your first UPI account, here's a story so you don't make my mistake, almost.
Last week a man called saying he was from a delivery company and wanted to refund me ₹499. He sent a QR code and said, 'Scan and enter your PIN to receive.' I was about to do it! Stay sharp,
Gargi didi

qa.q: What rule saved Gargi from the scam?

passage: So Sumit, you asked why I stopped lending money to people online. Listen. Last month, someone in a gaming group said he'd pay me double if I lent him five hundred for a tournament entry. He even sent a screenshot of 'payment sent' first. I checked my account. Nothing had come. The screenshot was fake. Then he got angry, saying, 'Send now, bro, it's urgent!' The pressure was the giveaway. I blocked him and told my mother. We reported the profile. After that I sat down and made a simple budget. Pocket money in, expenses out, and a small amount saved. Turns out I was spending most of it on game upgrades. I'm Mridul, sixteen, and now I check before I trust.

qa.q: Why did Mridul become suspicious of the stranger?
qa.a: Mridul's account showed no money, and the stranger's urgent pressure felt like a warning sign.

qa.q: What did Mridul do after spotting the fraud?
qa.a: Mridul blocked the stranger, told their mother, reported the profile and started a simple budget.

qa.q: How might Sumit use Mridul's story?

grounding: A teen recounts spotting fraud in online money requests and starting a simple budget.

passage: Two weeks before the panchayat election in their village near Nashik, a video began circulating: a candidate standing beside a new school building, captioned 'He built this!' Jeevan, seventeen, watched it three times at the tea stall. Something bothered him. The school looked exactly like the one in the next district. His sister Rashmi, nineteen and voting for the first time, asked, 'So should I vote for him?' 'Let's check first,' Jeevan said. They went to the gram panchayat office and asked to see the list of works done. The school wasn't on it. 'So the video is false?' 'This part is. Doesn't mean he's bad. Just check his real work, and the others' too.' Rashmi nodded and borrowed the list.

qa.q: How might Rashmi approach future campaign videos after this?

grounding: Shows a rural teen checking a political claim and learning how local elections and records work.

passage: In Johannesburg, Lindiwe, seventeen, was reading two news sites about the city council's vote to raise water tariffs. One headline said, 'Council Robs Residents!' The other said, 'Council Approves Tariff Change After Drought Warnings.' She frowned and messaged Sami from civics class: 'Same story, totally different vibe.' Sami replied, 'Check the actual council minutes. They're public.' That evening she found them online. Forty councillors had voted; the reasons were listed, and some had objected. She also found out her ward councillor's name for the first time. Lindiwe turns eighteen next year. She added a reminder on her phone: 'Register to vote.' Then she emailed her councillor a question about the drought plan.

qa.q: What were the two headlines Lindiwe read about the council?
qa.a: 'Council Robs Residents!' and 'Council Approves Tariff Change After Drought Warnings.'

qa.q: How did Lindiwe feel reading the two different headlines?
qa.a: She was puzzled and a bit suspicious, noticing the same story was told with very different emotion.

qa.q: Which of Lindiwe's steps could any young reader copy?
qa.a: Comparing sources, reading the original public record and contacting their representative with a question.

qa.q: How might Lindiwe's councillor see an email from a young resident?
qa.a: The councillor might be pleased, or at least reminded that young future voters are paying attention.

grounding: Shows a teen outside India reading news critically and learning how local governance and voting work.
